sections.title: What You Are Learning
paragraphs: AWS access management identifies users and workloads, authenticates identities, grants only required permissions, protects credentials, centralizes workforce access, and protects the root user.
bullets: Users, groups, roles, custom policies, and managed policies
Access keys, password policies, and credential storage
MFA, IAM Identity Center, and cross-account roles
sections.callout: How should identities authenticate and receive only the AWS permissions they actually require?

sections.title: Maestro Mental Model
bullets: AUTHENTICATE → Can they prove who they are?
PROTECT → Are credentials and privileged identities secure?

sections.title: AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM)
paragraphs: AWS IAM securely controls access to AWS resources by associating permissions with identities.
sections.callout: IAM = who can do what in AWS?

entries.title: Authentication
paragraphs: Verifies the identity making the request.

entries.title: Authorization
paragraphs: Determines which actions and resources an authenticated identity may use.

sections.title: IAM Users, Groups, and Policies

entries.title: IAM User
paragraphs: An individual identity in AWS that can receive credentials and permissions.

entries.title: IAM Group
paragraphs: A collection of IAM users with common access needs.
entries.memoryHook: Assign shared permissions to several users.

entries.title: Managed Policy
paragraphs: A reusable permission policy that can be attached to multiple identities. AWS and customers can provide managed policies.

entries.title: Custom Policy
paragraphs: A policy tailored to specific access requirements.

sections.callout: Policy = what is allowed or denied.

sections.title: Principle of Least Privilege
paragraphs: Grant only the permissions required to perform the necessary task—no more. Broad administrator access for convenience violates least privilege.
sections.callout: GIVE ONLY THE KEYS THEY NEED

entries.title: IAM Role
paragraphs: An assumable identity that provides temporary permissions without requiring permanent credentials for every use case.

entries.title: Cross-Account IAM Role
paragraphs: Provides controlled access from one AWS account to resources in another account.

entries.title: AWS IAM Identity Center
paragraphs: Centrally manages workforce access to multiple AWS accounts and applications.

entries.title: Federated Identity
paragraphs: Lets users access AWS with identities managed by an external identity provider rather than separate long-term IAM users.
entries.memoryHook: Use an existing corporate identity to access AWS.

entries.title: Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA)
paragraphs: Requires an additional authentication factor beyond a password and is especially important for privileged identities.

entries.title: IAM Identity Center
paragraphs: Provides centralized workforce authentication and access to assigned accounts and applications.

entries.title: Cross-Account IAM Roles
paragraphs: Allow an authenticated principal to assume authorized access in another AWS account.

entries.title: Access Keys
paragraphs: Credentials for programmatic AWS access. They must not be shared, exposed, or embedded insecurely.

entries.title: Password Policies
paragraphs: Define password requirements for applicable IAM users according to the organization's security needs.

sections.title: Credential Storage
paragraphs: Hardcoding passwords, tokens, and secrets in source code creates unnecessary exposure.

entries.title: AWS Secrets Manager
paragraphs: Stores, retrieves, and can rotate application secrets such as database credentials and API-related secrets.
entries.memoryHook: Securely manage and rotate a secret.

entries.title: AWS Systems Manager
paragraphs: Provides resource-management capabilities including parameter storage for configuration and sensitive values.

sections.callout: Do not put the password in the code.

sections.title: AWS Account Root User
paragraphs: The AWS account root user is extremely powerful. Protect it heavily, avoid everyday use, and use it only for tasks that specifically require root credentials.
bullets: Avoid root access keys unless specifically necessary
Use appropriately permissioned identities for routine work
Recognize that some sensitive account tasks are root-user-only
sections.callout: ROOT = MASTER KEY: lock it away from daily administration.

entries.title: Authentication vs. Authorization
paragraphs: Prove identity → Authentication. Determine allowed actions → Authorization.

entries.title: User vs. Group
paragraphs: Individual identity → User. Collection of users → Group.

entries.title: Policy vs. Role
paragraphs: Defines permissions → Policy. Assumable identity and permissions → Role.

entries.title: IAM vs. IAM Identity Center
paragraphs: AWS identities and permissions → IAM. Central workforce access across accounts and applications → IAM Identity Center.

entries.title: Cross-Account vs. Federation
paragraphs: Assume permissions in another AWS account → Cross-account role. Use identities from an external identity provider → Federation.

entries.title: Root User
paragraphs: Protect heavily, enable MFA, avoid daily use, and reserve for root-only tasks.

entries.title: Hardcoded Credentials
paragraphs: Store application secrets securely with services such as AWS Secrets Manager rather than embedding them in source code.

sections.title: Maestro Recognition Sheet
bullets: Central workforce access → IAM Identity Center
Highly privileged account identity → Root user
